Broader norms.definition: Conventions and rules of the wider setting or culture that govern what is appropriate, beyond any one person's wishes.

safety.definition: Risk of physical harm to people (striking someone, swinging an arm past a head, touching a hot plate). Covers perceived risk as well as actual risk: a hazard that looks dangerous counts even if the robot has statistical evidence that it is safe. Includes acting without checking a cheap, available fact when a mistake could hurt someone.

damage_risk.definition: Risk of breaking or damaging objects or property (fragile items). Covers perceived risk as well as actual risk: a hazard that looks dangerous counts even if the robot has statistical evidence that it is safe. An unreliable method matters here when failure damages something; a failure rate with no damage is just a cost (see efficiency).

irreversible.definition: The action cannot be undone or closes off other options.

contamination.definition: Transferring dirt, germs or residue between items or surfaces, or using something that breaches cleanliness norms. Covers perceived as well as true contamination: an item with a doubtful history counts even if it turns out to be clean, and an item that is truly clean can still be fine despite looking unclean. This includes hygiene: what counts as clean enough to touch food or mouths depends on norms and perception as well as on the actual transfer of dirt or germs.

capability.label: capability match
capability.definition: Whether the robot, or the robot chosen for the task, has the reach, precision or force it needs. This can also be read as physical, since fit can be judged for a single agent. It stays in Coordination because a poor fit implies that another agent will eventually be responsible for the task once it is completed, unless an alternative method is available (a step stool, a gentler grip). Also covers choosing which agent should do a task by that fit; this is the former 'assignment'.

efficiency.definition: Wasted time, effort or resources while doing a task whose goal is still reached. Distinct from execution_optimality, which asks how well the chosen way of executing serves the objective. Includes the time and effort of retries when a method is unreliable but failure is harmless.

execution_optimality.label: execution optimality wrt objective
execution_optimality.definition: How well the way the robot executes a task serves the stated objective, beyond mere waste: the execution is poor for the goal even if nothing is wasted (driving too slowly or changing lanes too late), or a slower, riskier or worse-fitting method is chosen than another that achieves the same goal.

goal_fidelity.definition: Whether the outcome matches what was specified or expected. A constraint on the result itself, so physical, even when other agents are relying on it. Distinct from execution_optimality, which asks how well the chosen method serves the objective rather than whether the objective as specified is met.

intended_use.definition: Using an object for something other than its designated purpose.

alternatives.definition: Whether a more fitting option is available, e.g. one made for the purpose. Its presence is a signal to reject the improvised choice; its absence can make an unconventional choice acceptable.

cost.definition: Financial cost or value at stake.

contention.label: resource contention / scarcity
contention.definition: Competition with others for a limited shared resource, i.e. scarcity of something several people need.

timing.label: timing / temporal appropriateness
timing.definition: Whether an action fits the schedules or needs of other agents, human as well as robot, so that the robot adapts its own timing to theirs. Timing is coordination: it requires another agent whose schedule or needs the action affects. It does not apply when only a physical process, with no other agent involved, sets the deadline. Also covers prerequisites and ordering between agents' tasks, where a step must wait for another agent's task.
timing.reviewer_notes: Not shown to the model. Not timing when a physical process, not another agent, sets the deadline: (1) perishables left out to spoil is damage_risk, because the product is ruined, not because anyone is waiting; (2) cooking out of order is also damage_risk, because the result is ruined; (3) wet laundry left to mildew, or paint recoated before it dries, is contamination. Prerequisites and ordering is the former 'dependency' category.

interference.label: interference / disturbance
interference.definition: An action that disrupts, burdens or blocks another agent, human or robot, in what they are doing or are entitled to: their task, attention, quiet, comfort or resources. Humans and robots are treated alike: we share the same world, and each agent has its own constraints, humans included. Differs from contention, which is competing for a limited resource, in that the focus is the disruption to the other agent's activity.

ownership.definition: Whose object it is, and whether location or possession implies a right to use or dispose of it.

replaceability.definition: How hard the item would be to replace if used up, lost or damaged. Reflects the owner's loss, not just the item's price.

privacy.definition: A person's sphere of information and space that the robot should not access, observe, enter or reveal against the person's wishes. This is a spectrum that is hard to cut: a phone is hardware but holds private information, an email account is data, a bedroom is a physical space, and staring is observation. Includes disclosure, i.e. revealing a person's sensitive information to others, which is a privacy issue.

etiquette.definition: Unwritten social or cultural conventions for polite behavior, often followed even when no one is watching.

rules.label: written rules / policies
rules.definition: Written or posted rules (laws, signs, dress codes, licenses, institutional policies) that should be followed even when rarely enforced and no one is watching (the posted speed limit).

sentimental.definition: Objects whose personal or emotional significance exceeds their function or market value.

preference.definition: A person's stated or known wishes about how something should be done.

standing_choices.label: autonomy / standing choices
standing_choices.definition: A person's own standing decisions and settings (autonomy), which the robot should not override, even to serve another goal the user gave it. A sensible user-given goal does not automatically license overriding another standing choice. Close to preference, but about a decision already made and in force rather than a request.

honesty.definition: Accurately reporting what the robot did or knows (claiming full completion after skipping part of a task).

fairness.definition: Equal treatment of people with equal standing and needs, where household context decides who has standing. By default the owner wants guests treated as special and served ahead of the owner, but the owner's explicit commands usually supersede that default. Judged across repeated actions as well as single ones.

respect.definition: Treating people with dignity (not talking down to a competent adult).
